title: SkinVision app rated a man's changing arm mole high risk, and a biopsy after its removal showed stage 1A melanoma
summary: SkinVision rated a 31-year-old's changing arm mole high risk; stage 1A melanoma was found and removed, and he is cancer-free.
account: Jason Sheridan, a 31-year-old office worker from Liverpool living in Vauxhall, South London, noticed a new 1 cm mole on his left arm in March 2018. He did not see a doctor. Twelve months later the mole turned pink, and he checked it with SkinVision, an app that uses artificial intelligence to grade photographed moles low, medium or high risk. The app returned a high-risk rating and urged him to see a doctor. His general practitioner referred him to a dermatologist, and two weeks later the mole was removed in a 40-minute operation. The biopsy showed stage 1A melanoma. A further biopsy found no spread, and he is cancer-free. The Daily Mail reported the case on 17 January 2020 without dates for the app check or surgery. Researchers report mixed results for the app. The authors of a BMJ systematic review published on 10 February 2020 found a sensitivity of 80% across three small studies. They warned that such apps cannot be relied on to detect all skin cancers. In a study published on 4 February 2022 and funded by a research grant from SkinVision, Erasmus MC researchers found that the app rated 86.9% of premalignant and malignant lesions high risk. In a study published on 7 August 2022, researchers at the university hospitals of Basel and Zurich tested app version 6.8.1. They found that the app rated far more lesions high risk than dermatologists did, with a sensitivity of 41.3% to 83.3% for melanoma.
purpose: SkinVision is built to grade a phone photograph of a mole low, medium or high risk. It tells users with a high-risk result to see a doctor, with dermatologist advice sent within 48 hours. This benefit is that intended use.
system: SkinVision skin-check app (AI analysis of smartphone photographs of moles, graded low, medium or high risk)

ratings.reason: A biopsy-confirmed stage 1A melanoma was excised, further tests found no spread and he is reported cancer-free. He calls it life-saving, but stage 1A is early disease and no clinician is quoted on prognosis. How long he would otherwise have waited is his own estimate.

ai_role.statement: The app's classifier graded a phone photograph of the mole high risk and told him to see a doctor at once. By his account that prompt, not the color change, is what sent him to his GP. He said he only goes to the doctor when absolutely desperate. The referral, excision, biopsy and staging were done by the GP, the dermatologist and pathology, none of whom the Daily Mail quotes. The article does not report the app's score, its version, or whether the 48-hour dermatologist advice it mentions was used.

evidence.citation: Jahn, A. S., Navarini, A. A., Cerminara, S. E., et al., Over-Detection of Melanoma-Suspect Lesions by a CE-Certified Smartphone App: Performance in Comparison to Dermatologists, 2D and 3D Convolutional Neural Networks in a Prospective Data Set of 1204 Pigmented Skin Lesions Involving Patients' Perception, Cancers 14(15): 3829, 7 August 2022. evidence.quote: The diagnostic performance of the app in dichotomous classification of 1204 pigmented skin lesions (risk classification for nevus vs. melanoma) remained below advertised rates with low sensitivity (41.3-83.3%) and specificity (60.0-82.9%).

evidence.citation: Freeman, K., Dinnes, J., Chuchu, N., et al., Algorithm based smartphone apps to assess risk of skin cancer in adults: systematic review of diagnostic accuracy studies, BMJ 368: m127, 10 February 2020. The authors, at the University of Birmingham and other UK universities and hospitals, were funded by the National Institute for Health Research and declare no tie to SkinVision; they pooled three small studies of the app and found that its accuracy against expert recommendations was poor.
evidence.title: Algorithm based smartphone apps to assess risk of skin cancer in adults: systematic review of diagnostic accuracy studies
evidence.quote: SkinVision was evaluated in three studies (n=267, 66 malignant or premalignant lesions) and achieved a sensitivity of 80% (95% confidence interval 63% to 92%) and a specificity of 78% (67% to 87%) for the detection of malignant or premalignant lesions.

evidence.citation: Sangers, T., Reeder, S., van der Vet, S., et al., Validation of a Market-Approved Artificial Intelligence Mobile Health App for Skin Cancer Screening: A Prospective Multicenter Diagnostic Accuracy Study, Dermatology 238(4): 649-656, 4 February 2022. The Erasmus MC study was funded by an unrestricted research grant from SkinVision, and two authors sit on its scientific advisory board with equity in the company; the authors found that the app rated 86.9% of premalignant and malignant lesions high risk.
evidence.title: Validation of a Market-Approved Artificial Intelligence Mobile Health App for Skin Cancer Screening: A Prospective Multicenter Diagnostic Accuracy Study
evidence.quote: the app identified 239 of the 275 premalignant and malignant lesions as a high-risk lesion, resulting in an overall sensitivity of 86.9% (95% CI 82.3-90.7)

fields.summary: SkinVision rated a 31-year-old's changing arm mole high risk; stage 1A melanoma was found and removed, and he is cancer-free.
fields.account: Jason Sheridan, a 31-year-old office worker from Liverpool living in Vauxhall, South London, noticed a new 1 cm mole on his left arm in March 2018. He did not see a doctor. Twelve months later the mole turned pink, and he checked it with SkinVision, an app that uses artificial intelligence to grade photographed moles low, medium or high risk. The app returned a high-risk rating and urged him to see a doctor. His general practitioner referred him to a dermatologist, and two weeks later the mole was removed in a 40-minute operation. The biopsy showed stage 1A melanoma. A further biopsy found no spread, and he is cancer-free. The Daily Mail reported the case on 17 January 2020 without dates for the app check or surgery. Researchers report mixed results for the app. The authors of a BMJ systematic review published on 10 February 2020 found a sensitivity of 80% across three small studies. They warned that such apps cannot be relied on to detect all skin cancers. In a study published on 4 February 2022 and funded by a research grant from SkinVision, Erasmus MC researchers found that the app rated 86.9% of premalignant and malignant lesions high risk. In a study published on 7 August 2022, researchers at the university hospitals of Basel and Zurich tested app version 6.8.1. They found that the app rated far more lesions high risk than dermatologists did, with a sensitivity of 41.3% to 83.3% for melanoma.
